title: User stories and epics: who, what and why
blurb: Write and recognize user stories, add acceptance criteria, split epics and see how sets of stories become work packages.
question: A product owner writes: 'As a commuter, I want to renew my season ticket on my phone so that I do not have to queue.' What three things does this format capture, and what must be added before the team can start work on it?

teach.h: A requirement told from the user's side
teach.body: User stories are a very popular way to document requirements in agile. The exact wording varies, but every story describes three things: who wants something, what they want, and why they want it (a format credited to Rachel Davies). The usual template is 'As a [who], I want [what], so that [why]'. Because the why is stated, the team can judge value and find better ways to meet the need.

steps.label: So that...
steps.sub: WHY: the value it gives them

steps.label: Acceptance criteria
steps.sub: How we will know it works

teach.h: Acceptance criteria make a story testable
teach.body: Acceptance criteria are the conditions a story must meet to be accepted. They should be clear, measurable and testable. A story counts as ready to start when it has its who, what and why plus measurable, prioritized acceptance criteria (Definition of Ready, 9.3.2.1). In the team planning workshop, the user story refinement topic makes sure criteria are clear and testable, and the tester later checks products against them and the team DoD.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 9.3.2.1; Table 13.13; Table B.1

root.label: Epic: manage my season ticket online
root.sub: large and vague, held in the project backlog

teach.caption: Each detailed story is small enough for a team to plan into an iteration.

teach.h: Epics: stories too big to plan yet
teach.body: Requirements often start large or vague. A story at that level is an epic (a term from Mike Cohn): a high-level story that breaks down into more detailed stories (8.3.2.2). The project backlog is made up mostly of epics. It is created in starting up a project, and the project canvas workshop scopes the project as epics prioritized with MoSCoW. Teams then split epics into the detailed stories that fill their product backlogs.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 8.3.2.1, 8.3.2.2; Tables 13.1 and 13.2

teach.body: In PRINCE2 Agile the project manager and product owner agree work as work package descriptions, and each one is a set of user stories. The team accepts it in managing product delivery and produces a team plan. When the work is finished, the project manager's 'receive completed work package' activity confirms that the set of stories (or the features agreed for the timebox) was delivered.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 7.3.1, Table 8.1, Tables 13.9 and 13.12

teach.h: From personas to a release map
teach.caption: A user story map is recommended instead of a product breakdown structure (8.3.1, 8.3.2.4).

teach.body: Product owner Tomasz Nowak takes the epic 'manage my season ticket online' from the project backlog. With help from the team coach, the team splits it into stories such as 'As a commuter, I want to renew my ticket on my phone, so that it does not lapse while I travel.' Acceptance criteria follow: renewal takes under two minutes and a confirmation email arrives. Tomasz and the project manager agree a set of these stories as the next work package.

teach.text: A user story is not a technical design or a task list: it states who, what and why, and acceptance criteria say how success is checked. An epic is not a different kind of requirement with its own owner: it is simply a story too big to plan, and it sits in the project backlog until it is split.

items: User story = who, what and why: 'As a..., I want..., so that...' (8.3.2.3).
Acceptance criteria make a story testable; a story is ready when it has them.
Epic = a large or vague story that breaks into detailed stories (8.3.2.2).
Project backlog: mostly epics (CPO). Product backlog: detailed stories (PO).
A work package description in PRINCE2 Agile is a set of user stories.
A user story map replaces the product breakdown structure.

summary: You can now recognize the who, what and why of a user story, explain what acceptance criteria add and how epics split into stories. You can also say where stories live and how a set of them forms a work package.

A.q: A user story is based on describing which three things?
A.why: User stories describe who wants something, what they want and why (Rachel Davies, book 8.3.2.3).

whyNot.1: How and when are planning and design matters; a story states who, what and why.
whyNot.2: Where and how much belong to plans (the plans practice), not to the story format.
whyNot.3: Why is right, but a story does not set when or how; it states who and what.

A.q: What is an epic user story?
options: A story that has met its Definition of Done
A large or vague story split into smaller stories
A story the CPO has prioritized as a Must have
A story shared by the work of two delivery teams
A.why: An epic is a high-level, large or vague user story that breaks down into more detailed user stories (8.3.2.2).

whyNot.0: Meeting the Definition of Done makes a story complete; it does not make it an epic.
whyNot.2: MoSCoW priority does not define an epic; an epic can carry any priority.
whyNot.3: Being shared across teams does not make a story an epic; size and vagueness do.

A.q: In PRINCE2 Agile, a work package description agreed between the project manager and the product owner typically takes the form of:
A.why: The PM and PO agree work as work package descriptions, which in PRINCE2 Agile are sets of user stories (7.3.1, Table 8.1).

whyNot.0: The team plan is what the delivery team produces after accepting the work package.
whyNot.1: A story map is a planning technique for breaking products into stories, not the work package itself.
whyNot.3: The project canvas is the business justification for the whole project.

B.q: What do acceptance criteria add to a user story?
options: The order in which the team will build it
The story points the team has estimated for it
The name of the developer who will build it next
Testable conditions it must meet to be accepted
B.why: Acceptance criteria set the conditions a story must meet to be accepted; they should be clear, measurable and testable (9.3.2.1, Table 13.13).

whyNot.0: Build order comes from backlog prioritization and iteration planning, not acceptance criteria.
whyNot.1: Story points come from effort estimation, a separate team planning topic.
whyNot.2: Stories describe the user's need; they do not assign a developer.

B.q:
Which two statements about user stories in PRINCE2 Agile are correct?
1. The project backlog is made up mostly of epic user stories.
2. User stories set out the technical design the developers must follow.
3. A story is ready when it has who, what and why plus measurable acceptance criteria.
4. User stories are a management product that replaces the business case.
B.why: The project backlog holds mostly epics (8.3.2.1), and the DoR example says a story is ready when it has who, what and why plus measurable, prioritized acceptance criteria (9.3.2.1).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is wrong: stories describe user needs, not technical design.
whyNot.2: Both 2 and 4 are wrong: the project canvas replaces the business case.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is wrong: the project canvas, not user stories, replaces the business case.

B.q: Which technique starts from personas, brainstorms user activities, puts them in chronological order and breaks them into user stories?
B.why: Story mapping starts from user descriptions or personas, brainstorms activities, orders them chronologically and breaks them into stories (8.3.2.4).

whyNot.1: Magic estimation sizes many items quickly; it does not create stories.
whyNot.2: A product flow diagram shows the sequence and dependencies of products.
whyNot.3: Delegation poker defines decision-making levels within a team.

C.q: Which role owns the product backlog holding a team's user stories, and which role owns the project backlog of epics?
C.why: The product owner owns a team's product backlog; the chief product owner owns the project backlog and sets priorities across teams (Table B.1).

whyNot.1: The team coach helps the team write stories but owns no backlog, and the executive does not own the project backlog.
whyNot.2: The project manager does not own a product backlog; that is the product owner.

C.q: Which statement about epics is correct?
options: They are created by each delivery team in its team planning workshop
They are high-level stories forming most of the project backlog
They replace user stories once a product backlog is approved
They are written by the tester to record defects found
C.why: Epics are high-level stories that break into detailed ones, and the project backlog consists mostly of epics (8.3.2.1, 8.3.2.2).

whyNot.0: The project backlog, including epics, is created in starting up a project, not in team planning.
whyNot.2: Epics are split into user stories; they do not replace them.
whyNot.3: Defects are not recorded as epics; an epic is a large requirement.

C.q: Which controlling a stage activity confirms that the set of user stories in a work package has been delivered?
C.why: In 'receive completed work package' the project manager confirms the team delivered the set of user stories, or the features agreed for the timebox (Table 13.9).

whyNot.0: Accepting a work package happens in managing product delivery, when the team takes the work on.
whyNot.1: Evaluating work package status monitors progress through conversations with the PO and the team dashboard; it does not confirm completion.
whyNot.3: Authorizing a work package is where the work is agreed and released to the team, before delivery.

reteach.title: Write it like a sticky note
reteach.question: How would you capture a need on a single sticky note so that anyone can see who it is for and why it matters?

blocks.body: Picture a sticky note with three slots: who (the user), what (the thing they need) and why (the value to them). On the back, write how you will check it works: those are the acceptance criteria. If the note is too big to finish in one iteration, it is an epic, so split it into smaller notes.

blocks.text: The 'so that' part is the WHY. Leaving it out removes the value the team needs to prioritize and design a good answer.

explain.body: A user story names who wants something, what they want and why, usually as 'As a..., I want..., so that...'. The why keeps the team focused on value.

test.q: In 'As a commuter, I want to renew my season ticket on my phone so that it does not lapse', which part gives the why?
options: I want to renew my season ticket on my phone
so that it does not lapse
test.why: The 'so that' clause states the value to the user: the why.

whyNot.1: 'I want to renew my season ticket on my phone' is the what.
whyNot.3: Acceptance criteria say how the story will be checked; they are not the why.

explain.body: Acceptance criteria are the testable conditions a story must meet to be accepted. They are part of being ready, are sharpened in the team planning workshop and are what the tester checks against.

test.q: In the team planning workshop, which topic makes sure acceptance criteria are clear and testable?
test.why: User story refinement makes acceptance criteria clear and testable and clarifies what counts as done (Table 13.13).

whyNot.0: Product backlog refinement clarifies and prioritizes the backlog with MoSCoW.
whyNot.2: Effort estimation builds a shared view of each story's complexity and effort.
whyNot.3: Iteration planning selects stories by priority and estimate for the team plan.

explain.body: An epic is a large or vague story that breaks into detailed stories. The project backlog, made up mostly of epics, is created in starting up a project; the project canvas workshop scopes the project as epics prioritized with MoSCoW.

test.q: In which process is the project backlog, including its epics, first created?
test.why: In starting up a project, the PM with the CPO, senior supplier and executive defines what is to be delivered and creates the project backlog, including epics (Table 13.1).

whyNot.1: Initiating a project may update the project backlog, but it is first created in starting up.
whyNot.2: Managing product delivery works from product backlogs; it does not create the project backlog.
whyNot.3: A stage boundary updates the release map; the project backlog already exists.

explain.body: The PM and PO agree a work package as a set of user stories. The team accepts it and produces a team plan, delivers the stories, and the PM confirms delivery in 'receive completed work package'.

test.q: What does the delivery team produce when it accepts a set of user stories as a work package?
test.why: When accepting a work package, the team reviews the stories and produces a team plan of what it can complete within the constraints (Table 13.12).

whyNot.0: The release map is the project and stage plan, updated by the project manager.
whyNot.1: An exception report is raised when a stage or project is forecast to exceed tolerance.
whyNot.2: The project canvas is the project-level business justification.
